card.intuition: A memory system makes an agent stateful across sessions by persisting what it learns to the filesystem during a session and reloading it at the start of future ones. The model itself is stateless, so this memory layer fakes continuity.
card.analogy: A consultant who writes a one-page brief after every client meeting and re-reads it before the next call, instead of starting from a blank slate each time.
card.time_complexity: O(loaded tokens per turn): everything reloaded into the context window is billed as input on every request, so always-loaded memories must stay lean to keep operational cost flat.
card.space_complexity: O(one-line index + pointers): the context window is finite, so keep a one-line index in context and leave the memory bodies behind context pointers rather than inlining everything.
when_to_use: When you keep re-telling the agent the same project facts, like the database being Postgres not MySQL
When you want continuity to survive the user clearing the session
When using a harness that ships its own memory system, or building a directory of notes plus an AGENTS.md instruction
gotchas: Memories are secondary sources and drift — a fact recorded in March is loaded with equal confidence in June after the project moved on
Memories accumulate and bloat the context window if they are not pruned
The facade of continuity can mask staleness when the read path reloads outdated files

steps.label: Record
steps.annotation: During the session the agent persists a learned preference or fact as a file in the environment.

steps.label: Index
steps.annotation: A one-line index points at each memory body so that reloading stays cheap.

steps.label: Reload
steps.annotation: At session start the harness loads the index, or the bodies, back into the context window.

steps.label: Prune
steps.annotation: Memories drift over time, so pruning removes entries the project has moved past.

exercise.prompt: Write a function that loads a memory index and returns the body path for a matching memory key. It must return None when the key is absent.
hints: The key may not be present, so guard the lookup before returning anything
A missing memory should evaluate falsy, so None keeps downstream checks clean
exercise.test_code:
index = {'db': 'mysql:notes/db.md', 'oncall': 'notes/oncall.md'}
assert lookup(index, 'db') == 'mysql:notes/db.md'
assert lookup(index, 'missing') is None
print('PASS')
